The last time I stood in a room and did nothing was probably in an elevator, and even then I was looking at a screen. The phone came out of my pocket like a reflex, a small smooth rectangle of infinite distraction, and I scrolled through a feed of people I do not know doing things I do not care about until the doors opened. By the time I reached the sidewalk I had already forgotten what I had seen. This is the texture of contemporary life: a continuous, low-grade forgetting punctuated by the occasional jolt of outrage or tenderness.

There is a myth that we are living in an age of unprecedented information. It is half true. We are certainly living in an age of unprecedented *access* to information, but the human mind has always been crowded. A medieval monk copying manuscripts in a scriptorium had to contend with the noise of the wind, the irregularities of vellum, the memory of a conversation in the cloister, the ache in his hand, and the perpetual temptation to think about God, or dinner, or both. What has changed is not the quantity of attention but the architecture of interruption. The interruptions used to be environmental and social; now they are engineered, personalized, and monetized. Every application is a little machine designed to capture the wandering mind and keep it wandering in a profitable direction.

Memory, as a consequence, has become curatorial. We no longer need to remember facts because we can search for them; we no longer need to remember faces because they are archived in photographs; we no longer need to remember the way to a place because a voice will tell us when to turn. This is enormously convenient. It is also quietly erosive. The act of remembering is not merely a retrieval; it is a re-creation. Each time we call something back, we change it slightly, we weave it into the present self, we make it ours. When we outsource memory to external systems, we lose some of that friction. The memory becomes flat, a file in a cabinet rather than a room we walk through.

And yet I am not interested in a simple lament. Nostalgia for a pre-digital past is too easy, and usually inaccurate. People have always complained about the speed of modern life; the ancient Romans worried that the invention of writing would destroy memory, and Socrates was hardly alone in thinking that literacy would make the mind lazy. The printing press, the telegraph, the radio, and television were all greeted with prophecies of cognitive decline. Some of those prophecies were not wrong, exactly, but they were incomplete. New technologies do not simply damage old capacities; they redistribute them. The question is always: what do we gain, what do we lose, and can we choose how to use the gain?

One thing we gain is a kind of democratized memory. A person with a smartphone can, in seconds, access photographs of their childhood, translations of ancient poems, the names of strangers, the history of a street. The archive is no longer guarded by priests, librarians, or wealthy collectors. The old hierarchy of memory—where proximity, class, and institutional power determined who could remember what—has been flattened. There is something genuinely beautiful in this. A teenager in Jakarta can watch a film made in Senegal in 1970 and be changed by it. A grandparent can see the face of a great-grandparent they never met. These are not small things.

What we lose, I think, is temporal depth. The present becomes swollen and the past becomes a resource. Everything is available, but availability is not the same as presence. I can listen to any music ever recorded, and as a result I sometimes listen to none of it with the intensity I once brought to a single album I saved for and played until the cassette warped. There is a difference between having access to a cathedral and living in one. The abundance of choice can make the chosen thing feel provisional.

There is also the matter of attention as a moral quality. Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. To attend to someone is to offer them the most finite thing we have: the present moment, unrepeatable, irretrievable. When we give our attention carelessly, we give ourselves carelessly. When we are perpetually half-present, we are perpetually half-ourselves. This is not a matter of productivity, though it affects productivity. It is a matter of love. To love someone, or something, is to consent to be interrupted by them. The child tugging on your sleeve, the friend who needs to talk, the tree that suddenly looks magnificent in the late light—these interruptions are the substance of a life. But if our attention is already fragmented by devices designed to exploit it, we have less to give when the real interruption comes.

The trick, of course, is not to destroy the machines but to learn to put them down. This is harder than it sounds because the machines are designed to be hard to put down. They exploit the same psychological mechanisms that make gambling addictive: variable rewards, intermittent reinforcement, the illusion of progress, the fear of missing out. The people who built these systems often do not let their own children use them, which tells you something. We are not in a fair fight. But we are not powerless either. We can choose, at least some of the time, to look up.

I try to remind myself that boredom is not an enemy. Boredom is the fertile ground from which attention grows. When the mind is not immediately sedated by novelty, it begins to wander, and wandering is where the real work happens: connections form, problems solve themselves, memories resurface, and the self reassembles. The mind without boredom is like a field without fallow seasons: it may produce constantly, but eventually the soil thins. Children who are never bored become adults who are never still. Adults who are never still become strangers to themselves.

I do not know what the future of attention will be. Perhaps we will develop new forms of discipline, new rituals, new technologies that protect us from the old ones. Perhaps we will not, and the average depth of human attention will continue to shrink until we become a civilization of skimmers, reacting to headlines without ever reading the article. Or perhaps the pendulum will swing, and slowness will become a luxury good, like clean air or quiet, available only to those who can afford it.

What I believe is this: the quality of our lives will be determined, more than by anything else, by the quality of our attention. Not by what we own, or what we achieve, or even by what happens to us, but by what we allow ourselves to notice, to feel, to remember. The world is full of astonishing things. The problem is not that they are hidden; the problem is that we are distracted. The cure is not to become ascetics, but to become deliberate. To choose, again and again, where to look. To let the phone stay in the pocket, the elevator ride be silent, and the mind remember what it is like to be alone with itself.

That is a kind of freedom, and it is still available.
